questions.subject: history_civics
questions.question_text: Mention any two ways in which the Constitution ensures the independence of the Judiciary from the Executive.
key_points: The judiciary and executive are involved in the appointment of the judges/judges can be removed only through impeachment
They have the security of tenure and can remain in office until they are 65 years of age
Their salaries are from the Consolidated Fund of India and not subject to vote of the Parliament
They have the freedom to announce decrees and decisions/their decisions cannot be criticized in public
They can punish anyone for contempt of court
The state has to ensure their safety
The court has full control over its work and establishment
No discussion can take place in the legislature on the conduct of any judge
Judges are prohibited from practising after retirement
Salaries are reduced only during financial emergency

factual_anchors.context: the retirement age securing judges' tenure, a valid independence point
judges' salaries charged on it, a valid independence point

questions.scheme_text: The judiciary and executive are involved in the appointment of the judges/judges can be removed only through impeachment /they have the security of tenure and can remain in office until they are 65 years of age/their salaries are from the Consolidated Fund of India and not subject to vote of the Parliament/they have the freedom to announce decrees and decisions/their decisions cannot be criticized in public/they can punish anyone for contempt of court/the state has to ensure their safety/The court has full control over its work and establishment / No discussion can take place in the legislature on the conduct of any judge/ judges are prohibited from practising after retirement/. Salaries are reduced only during financial emergency. (Any two points)
questions.model_answer: The Constitution safeguards judicial independence by giving judges security of tenure, so that they can remain in office until the age of 65 and can be removed only through impeachment; and by charging their salaries to the Consolidated Fund of India, which is not subject to a vote in Parliament.
questions.examiner_comment: Most of the candidates were not able to answer this question. They were not clear with the concept of 'Independence of Judiciary' from the 'Executive'.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Explain the necessity to maintain the independence of the judiciary for the functioning of a democracy.

questions.subject: history_civics

questions.scheme_text: Introduction of bills/act as a source of information /move amendments to the Constitution/ summon houses of Parliament through the President/prepare the special address of the President/advise the President to issue ordinances. (Any two points)
questions.model_answer: Two legislative powers of the Cabinet are the introduction of bills in Parliament, and advising the President to promulgate ordinances when Parliament is not in session.
questions.examiner_comment: Majority of the candidates got confused between the 'legislative' and 'executive powers'. Most chose policy making as a 'legislative power'. Several candidates were not able to attempt this question properly as they wrote 'Administrative powers' in place of 'Legislative powers'.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Differentiate between the various powers of the Union Cabinet. Explain the meaning of the words Legislation, Legislative and Executive powers of the Cabinet and Parliament in detail through a classification chart.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.question_text: Give two reasons for the acceptance of the Mountbatten Plan by the Congress.
key_points: It was a solution to the large scale communal riots
The League had joined the interim government to obstruct and not cooperate
The only alternative to partition was a federation with a weak centre
Further continuity of British rule would mean a greater calamity
Not agreeing to the partition many result in the creation of many Pakistans
Further delay could lead to a civil war
Partition would help get rid of separate electorates and other undemocratic procedures
Result of Direct Action Day
A small India with a strong centre was better than a bigger state with a weak centre
British were encouraging the rulers of Indian states to remain Independent

factual_anchors.context: its aftermath is a listed reason for accepting the Plan
the plan whose acceptance is being tested

questions.scheme_text: It was a solution to the large scale communal riots/the League had joined the interim government to obstruct and not cooperate/ the only alternative to partition was a federation with a weak centre/further continuity of British rule would mean a greater calamity/not agreeing to the partition many result in the creation of many Pakistans/further delay could lead to a civil war/partition would help get rid of separate electorates and other undemocratic procedures./ Result of Direct action day/ A small India with a strong centre was better than a bigger state with a weak centre / British were encouraging the rulers of Indian states to remain Independent. (Any two points)
questions.model_answer: The Congress accepted the Mountbatten Plan because it offered a solution to the large-scale communal riots sweeping the country, and because the only alternative to partition was a federation with a dangerously weak centre.
questions.examiner_comment: This question was well attempted by all candidates. Few candidates wrote generalized answers.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Prepare a classification chart to clarify and teach students the difference between the Indian Independence Act, 1947 and the Mountbatten Plan - its clauses and reasons for its acceptance.

questions.teacher_suggestion: Guide students to understand the views of both the Muslim League and the Congress separately. Clearly define objectives of the various parties and organisations with examples.

Had to supply coal to France, Italy and Belgium for 10 years
The area of the Rhine valley was demilitarized
It was to be occupied by the Allied forces for 15 years

Eupen-et-Malmedy to Belgium
Schleswig to Denmark
Danzig became a free port in the Polish territory
The Saar coal mines were ceded to France

German colonies in the Pacific were given to Japan

The air force and submarines were banned

the treaty whose clauses are being tested

(Any two points)
questions.model_answer: Two clauses of the Treaty of Versailles were that Germany was declared guilty of aggression and made to pay war reparations of 33 billion dollars, and that Germany lost the territory of Alsace-Lorraine to France.
questions.examiner_comment: Most of the candidates answered this question correctly.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Discuss in detail the Treaty of Versailles its main clauses and how it became a cause for the Second World War.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: The Union Legislature comprises the President and the two houses of the Parliament. With reference to the Parliament, answer the following questions:

key_points: Must be a citizen of India
Must be at least 25 years of age
Should have his/her name in the electoral rolls in some part of the country
Should not be an insolvent
Should not hold any office of profit under the government
Should not be a proclaimed criminal
Should not be of unsound mind
Must have qualifications prescribed by parliament from time to time

Can make laws in the state list when there is an emergency or when two or more states request it or Rajya Sabha approves it by 2/3 majority
Can approve ordinances

the Rajya Sabha majority enabling legislation on state subjects

(Any three points)
questions.model_answer: Three legislative powers of the Union Parliament are the power to make laws on subjects in the Union List, on subjects in the Concurrent List, and to legislate on a State subject during a national emergency.
questions.examiner_comment: Many candidates attempted this question well. However, some candidates got confused and mentioned different powers.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: The Union Legislature comprises the President and the two houses of the Parliament. With reference to the Parliament, answer the following questions:
questions.question_text: The Parliament controls the Executive. Mention any four ways in which it exercises its control.
key_points: Through interpellation during question hour
Through question, discussions and debates
Through a vote of no-confidence
Adjournment motion
Through other motions of censure
Rejection of a Government Bill
Passing of a Private Member Bill against the wishes of the Government
Cut motion
Examining the reports of the Auditor-General

Monetary control
Debates

a vote of it is a listed control mechanism over the executive
examining its reports is a listed control mechanism

(Any four points)
questions.model_answer: Parliament exercises control over the Executive through interpellation during Question Hour, through debates and discussions on government policy, through a vote of no-confidence, and by examining the reports of the Auditor-General.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: The President is the head of the State and exercises his / her powers on the advice of the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers. With reference to this, answer the following questions:
questions.question_text: What are the three types of emergencies that can be proclaimed by the President?
key_points: National or General Emergency / civil war/threat to security/ insurgency/war/external aggression/internal disturbance/armed rebellion
Financial Emergency / threat to the credit of India/financial crisis/financial instability

Emergency due to Breakdown of Constitutional Machinery / State Emergency / Government report to the President / Government cannot function according to Constitution/State Government is unable to control law and order

factual_anchors.context: one of the three required types of emergency
one of the three required types of emergency
one of the three required types of emergency

questions.scheme_text: National or General Emergency/ civil war/threat to security/ insurgency/war/external aggression/internal disturbance/armed rebellion/Financial Emergency/ threat to the credit of India/financial crisis/financial instability/ Emergency due to Breakdown of Constitutional Machinery / State Emergency / Government report to the President /Government cannot function according to Constitution/State Government is unable to control law and order. (Any three points)
questions.model_answer: The three types of emergencies that the President can proclaim are a National Emergency, arising from war or external aggression; a Financial Emergency, arising from a threat to the financial stability of India; and an Emergency due to the breakdown of constitutional machinery in a State.
questions.examiner_comment: Most of the candidates answered this question correctly. Some candidates did not name the emergency but described the circumstances under which the emergencies be proclaimed. Few candidates wrote the impact and time period of each emergency instead of the types of emergencies.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Explain Emergency names with circumstances and relevant examples.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: The President is the head of the State and exercises his / her powers on the advice of the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers. With reference to this, answer the following questions:
questions.question_text: Mention any three legislative powers of the President.
key_points: Addresses the first session of the Parliament
Sends messages to the Parliament
Can summon and prorogue the Parliament
Can dissolve the Lok Sabha
Nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha
Gives assent to a bill to make it a law
Can promulgate ordinances
Can give his/her assent to some state bills
Previous sanction to the Money bills
Introduction of Bills
Give approval for introduction of Bills regarding alteration of State/formation of state
Can call for a joint session of parliament

factual_anchors.context: the number the President nominates to the Rajya Sabha
the House to which the President nominates members

questions.scheme_text: Addresses the first session of the Parliament/sends messages to the Parliament/can summon and prorogue the Parliament/can dissolve the Lok Sabha /nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha/gives assent to a bill to make it a law/can promulgate ordinances/can give his/her assent to some state bills /Previous sanction to the Money bills /Introduction of Bills/Give approval for introduction of Bills regarding alteration of State /formation of state. Can call for a joint session of parliament. (Any three points)
questions.model_answer: Three legislative powers of the President are addressing the first session of Parliament after each general election, summoning and proroguing Parliament and dissolving the Lok Sabha, and giving assent to a bill before it becomes a law.
questions.examiner_comment: Many candidates got confused between the Legislative and Executive powers of the President due to lack of clarity on powers of the President of India.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Clearly define Legislative and Executive powers and Executive powers while sharing various powers of the President of India.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: The President is the head of the State and exercises his / her powers on the advice of the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers. With reference to this, answer the following questions:
questions.question_text: Give any two reasons to justify the need for indirect election of the President. What is the composition of the Electoral College which elects the President?
key_points: Saves money and time
If elected directly he/she would become a rival to the Prime Minister
The President is just a nominal head
It would be difficult for the whole country to vote for one position
Difficult to provide electoral machinery
India has a parliamentary government
Majority of the population is illiterate
Election of the president is dignified procedure
President will become nominee of the ruling party, so states are also allowed to vote
Electoral College: The Members of the Parliament / The Members of the State Legislative Assemblies

factual_anchors.context: the body electing the President; central to the answer
a component of the Electoral College
a component of the Electoral College

questions.scheme_text: Need for indirect election (Two points): Saves money and time/if elected directly he /she would become a rival to the Prime Minister/the President is just a nominal head/it would be difficult for the whole country to vote for one position /difficult to provide electoral machinery/India has a parliamentary government/Majority of the population is illiterate/Election of the president is dignified procedure/President will become nominee of the ruling party, so states are also allowed to vote. Electoral College: The Members of the Parliament / The Members of the State Legislative Assemblies.
questions.model_answer: Indirect election of the President saves money and time compared to a nationwide direct election, and prevents the President — who is meant to be a nominal head — from becoming a political rival to the Prime Minister. The Electoral College that elects the President is composed of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies.
questions.examiner_comment: This question was well attempted by the candidates. Instead of two reasons, majority of the candidates had only described one reason for indirect election of the President. A few candidates misunderstood the question as they mentioned about the procedure of election. The composition of Electoral College for the President was answered well be most of the candidates.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Mention clearly that the President of India is not elected directly by the people since India has a Parliamentary form of Government. Explain the meaning in detail for procedural terms such as Electoral College and so on.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: The Constitution of India provides for a High Court for each State. With reference to the High Courts and Subordinate Courts, answer the following questions:
questions.question_text: Who appoints the judges of the High Court? Mention any two qualifications required for a person to be appointed as a judge of a High Court.
key_points: The President appoints judges of the High Court
Must be a citizen of India
Must not be above 62 years
Must have held a judicial office in India for at least 10 years
Must have been a High Court advocate for at least 10 years

factual_anchors.context: the appointing authority for High Court judges; the required answer
the retirement age, a valid qualification-related detail
the judicial-office or advocacy experience required

questions.scheme_text: The President. Qualifications - must be a citizen of India/must not be above 62 years/Must have held a judicial office in India for at least 10 years/must have been a High Court advocate for at least 10 years. (Any two points)
questions.model_answer: Judges of the High Court are appointed by the President. To be appointed, a person must be a citizen of India, and must have held a judicial office in India, or been a High Court advocate, for at least 10 years.
questions.examiner_comment: Most of the candidates answered the first part correctly but a few candidates were confused and mentioned about 'Chief Justice and Governor' instead of the 'President'. In the second part of the question about qualifications required for a judge, some of the candidates were confused between the qualifications of the High and Supreme Court judges.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Help students understand the difference between qualifications required for a judge of the Supreme Court and the High Court using tabular comparative table. Clearly explain appointments, qualifications, related terms, and jurisdictions of Supreme Court and High court.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: The Constitution of India provides for a High Court for each State. With reference to the High Courts and Subordinate Courts, answer the following questions:
questions.question_text: Mention any three cases that come under the Original Jurisdiction of the High Court.
key_points: State revenue and its collection
Cases regarding wills
Divorce, marriage, and company law
Contempt of court
Interpretation of constitution
Enforcement of Fundamental Rights
Election petitions challenging election of members
Protection of minorities
Admirality

factual_anchors.context: their enforcement is a case under original jurisdiction

questions.scheme_text: State revenue and its collection/cases regarding wills / divorce, marriage, / and company law/contempt of court/interpretation of constitution/enforcement of Fundamental Rights/election petitions challenging election of members / Protection of minorities/Admirality. (Any three points)
questions.model_answer: Cases under the Original Jurisdiction of the High Court include disputes over State revenue and its collection, cases regarding wills, divorce, marriage and company law, and cases relating to the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
questions.examiner_comment: Majority of the candidates responded correctly even though some candidates were confused between the 'High Court' and the 'Supreme Court' cases. The common errors made were regarding all civil cases and criminal cases mentioned instead of specific examples of cases that are a part of the original jurisdiction of High Court.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: The Constitution of India provides for a High Court for each State. With reference to the High Courts and Subordinate Courts, answer the following questions:
questions.question_text: What are Lok Adalats? Mention any three advantages of the Lok Adalats.
key_points: People's court or Court of People
Provide quick legal aid/eliminate high cost
Works on the spirit of compromise
Reduces the burden of the high courts
Decision is final
Can pass sentences in pre litigation stage
Cases can be filed by giving petition in plain paper
No complication
Person can argue his case without the help of lawyers
Promote social justice

factual_anchors.context: the institution the question is built around

questions.scheme_text: People's court or Court of People. Advantages - provide quick legal aid/eliminate high cost /works on the spirit of compromise/ reduces the burden of the high courts. decision is final/can pass sentences in pre litigation stage/cases can be filed by giving petition in plain paper/no complication/person can argue his case without the help of lawyers/promote social justice. (Any three points)
questions.model_answer: Lok Adalats, or 'People's Courts', are forums that provide quick and inexpensive legal aid, working on the spirit of compromise so that both parties reach a settlement. Their advantages include reducing the burden on the regular courts, allowing cases to be filed on a plain paper, and giving decisions that are final and binding on both parties.
questions.examiner_comment: This question was answered correctly by most of the candidates, even though, some candidates could not define the term 'Lok Adalat' and a few candidates mentioned about village panchayats.
questions.teacher_suggestion: Define 'Lok Adalats' as a Court of People and its advantages with examples.

questions.subject: history_civics
questions.parent_question_text: Look at the picture given below and answer the following questions:

British government agreed to: withdraw all ordinances and end prosecutions
British government agreed to: release all political prisoners except those guilty of violence
